sections.html:
Minot is both the seat and the largest city of Ward County, in north-central North Dakota. The 2020 census put the county at 69,919 people, fourth in the state. Berthold, Burlington, Carpio, Des Lacs, Donnybrook, Douglas, Kenmare, Makoti, Ryder, Sawyer and Surrey are the other incorporated cities, and farmland covers most of the ground outside them.

Minot Air Force Base employs the most people in the county, an estimated 6,957 on base, and more than 11,000 are tied to it once families and civilian staff are counted. Because service members relocate on orders, a base-connected seller often needs a closing date to plan around.

sections.h2: How a Ward County house is taxed
sections.html:
Take the true and full value of the house and keep 4.5 percent of it: that is the taxable value. Multiply it by the combined mill levy of every district taxing the parcel. One mill equals one tenth of one percent, so taxable value times 0.001 times the mills on your statement gives the tax. The state's residential property tax page describes it.

Half of market value counts as assessed value. A building with separate living quarters for fewer than four family units is residential, while apartment buildings of four or more units are commercial. The treasurer's statement lists the actual mills for your district.

The state offers a primary residence credit, and a homestead property tax credit that comes with a renter's refund. Each has eligibility rules on the state tax site. A seller who has claimed one should know the buyer has to qualify separately.

Real estate tax comes due on January 1 after the tax year ends, and the first installment turns delinquent once March 1 passes. The treasurer works from chapter 57-20 of the Century Code.

DateWhat happens
January 1Taxes for the prior tax year become due.
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount (paid or postmarked).
March 1First installment is delinquent after this date; a 3 percent penalty applies.
May 1Another 3 percent penalty is added to unpaid first-installment taxes.
July 1Another 3 percent penalty is added.
October 15Second installment is delinquent after this date, with a 6 percent penalty; unpaid first-installment taxes pick up a further 3 percent.

Only general real estate taxes paid in full by February 15 get the discount, and the treasurer applies it ahead of any primary residence credit. Personal property taxes and special assessment installments are excluded. After a weather or other catastrophe emergency declaration, commissioners may add 30 days to the discount period. Mobile homes follow the same discount rule, and statements are printed already reflecting the discount when payment in full comes by February 15.

Not receiving a statement doesn't excuse the bill. The county's property tax page offers payment online by credit card or e-check.

Begin at the Tax Equalization office, 225 Third St. SE, Suite 232, Minot 58701, 701-857-6430. When the assessor can't resolve your concern, the path runs through the local board of equalization in April, then the county board, and finally the State Board of Equalization.

Township boards meet the second Monday in April. Minot's City Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday of April, on a schedule set by the county tax director, and the city contact is 701-857-4108. Meeting dates can move, so verify them yearly.

The state board requires proof under NDCC 57-13-04.3 that you went to the local and county boards first. After that, write to propertytax@nd.gov or call the State Property Tax division at 701-328-3127 to open a state appeal, which involves a questionnaire and supporting evidence.

  • Collect recent comparable sales and any appraisal you have.
  • Take photos of defects the assessor might not know about.
  • Bring the notice and your parcel number to the April meeting.

Cold is a real inspection topic. Record lows hit minus 49 degrees Fahrenheit in February and minus 47 in January, which wears on furnaces, pipes and roofs in older houses.

In the 2011 Souris River flood, more than 4,000 Minot homes were flooded and about 11,000 people were evacuated. A buyout program afterward sought to give people with damaged or bought-out homes access to affordable housing. Flood insurance premiums and upcoming FEMA map changes remain live topics. Near the river, buyers will ask about flood zone status and insurance cost. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can price in that uncertainty, so you don't have to settle it before closing.

sections.h2: What to do before you list
sections.html:
A little homework with the county saves time later. Work through this order.

  1. Find your latest statement and check whether you paid in full by February 15 for the discount, or whether a March 1, May 1 or July 1 penalty has already been added.
  2. Call the treasurer for a payoff figure for the day you expect to close.
  3. If you disagree with the valuation, remember the April board meetings and the sequence from local board to county board to state.
  4. List any special assessments on the parcel, since they get no discount.
  5. Write down any primary residence or homestead credit you've been using, so you and the title company know what changes after the sale.

Owners near the Souris River should also pull their flood repair records, because buyers and insurers often ask for them.

The tax debt stays on the property, so it's usually paid from your proceeds at closing. Your title company orders a tax search and asks the treasurer for what's owed, including penalties accrued since March 1 or October 15.

Penalties accumulate by date. A summer seller who skipped March 1 would carry the first 3 percent plus the May 1 and July 1 additions. Paying before the next date stops the next penalty, and a payoff quoted for a particular day removes surprises.

  • Request a written payoff from the treasurer or title officer that stays good through your closing date.
  • Look for special assessments, which can't take the 5 percent discount.
  • Find out whether a primary residence or homestead credit you used ends at the sale.

A cash sale uses the same steps without a lender's underwriting, which can delay payoff.

Cash Home Buyers can review a Ward County house with back tax and explain how an as-is offer works, and you owe nothing if you decline. The title company pays the treasurer from your proceeds.

faqs.q: When is the Ward County property tax discount deadline?
faqs.a: February 15. Pay the year's real estate taxes in full by then, or have the payment postmarked by that date, to receive 5 percent off under NDCC 57-20-09.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Ward County taxes online?
faqs.a: Yes, by credit card or e-check. Look at the county's online payments page before you mail anything.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Ward County assessment?
faqs.a: Start with the Tax Equalization office, then the township or city board of equalization in April, then the county board. A state appeal is only available after you've applied to the local and county boards.

faqs.q: What is the penalty if I miss March 1?
faqs.a: A 3 percent penalty hits the first installment after March 1, and more 3 percent additions follow on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment carries 6 percent if it's unpaid by October 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Ward County house that still has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the unpaid amount and any penalty from the proceeds at closing, so a cash sale can close on your timeline.
